content.study:
Topic at a Glance
Article 124 of the Constitution of India is titled “Establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court”. It forms an integral component of The Union (Articles 52–151), located within the “Union Judiciary” cluster. Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023.

Constitutional Text & Anatomy
(1) There shall be a Supreme Court of India consisting of a Chief Justice of India and, until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number, of not more than [seven other Judges.

(2) Every Judge of the Supreme Court shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal on the recommendation of the National Judicial Appointments Commission referred to in article 124A and shall hold office until he attains the age of sixty-five years: [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted Provided that]—

(a) a Judge may, by writing under his hand addressed to the President, resign his office;

(b) a Judge may be removed from his office in the manner

provided in clause (4). omitted by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 16 . Now “thirty-three” vide the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019 (37 of 2019), such of the Judges of the Supreme Court and of the High Court in the States as the President may deem necessary for the purpose" .

Constituent Assembly Intent & Doctrinal Foundation
The framers envisioned Article 124 as a fundamental structural instrument. In constitutional jurisprudence, every clause operates not in isolation but as part of an integrated, transformative organic document. Key aspect: The 99th Amendment’s NJAC was struck down in 2015. The Three Judges Cases govern appointments.

Procedural & Courtroom Anchors (Senior Counsel Checklist)
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing & Remedial Path: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.
4. Evidentiary Standards: Where disputed facts or legislative arbitrariness are alleged, evidentiary burdens under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA ss. 104–106) and official gazette notifications govern the record.

Key Statutory Ingredients to Establish
1. (1) There shall be a Supreme Court of India consisting of a Chief Justice of India and, until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number, of not more than [seven other Judges.
2. (2) Every Judge of the Supreme Court shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal on the recommendation of the National Judicial Appointments Commission referred to in article 124A and shall hold office until he attains the age of sixty-five years: [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted Provided that]—
3. (a) a Judge may, by writing under his hand addressed to the President, resign his office;
4. (b) a Judge may be removed from his office in the manner

Judicial Interpretation & Binding Ratios
1. Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) (2016) 5 SCC 1: Struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act. Judicial primacy in appointments is part of the basic structure. The collegium system revived.

Current-Law Position & Milestone
Current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. Any attempt by subordinate legislation or executive notifications to abridge the mandate of Article 124 is subject to judicial review under Articles 226 and 32.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Direct Application (Constitutional Guarantee / Power Upheld)
examples.body: State action or statutory exercise strictly satisfies the conditions laid down under Article 124 (Establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court). The authority acts within constitutional bounds, respects procedural fairness, and advances the constitutional objective of Union Judiciary. Outcome: Action is held valid and enforceable by the Court.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Boundary Condition / Breach (State Action Fails)
examples.body: An executive order or legislation violates or bypasses the express procedural conditions, jurisdictional threshold, or fundamental guarantees of Article 124. The action is tainted by manifest arbitrariness, lacks legislative competence, or ignores mandatory safeguards. Outcome: The Court strikes down the measure or issues a writ of certiorari / mandamus.

hypotheticals.question: Examine the constitutional validity of the impugned directive in light of Article 124 and settled Supreme Court jurisprudence. What relief, if any, can be granted?
hypotheticals.analysis:
1. Scrutinize the constitutional source of power: Does Article 124 grant plenary power, or is it conditioned by express safeguards, legislative competence, or fundamental rights?
2. Apply the doctrine of ultra vires and manifest arbitrariness: If the directive creates arbitrary exceptions or bypasses statutory provisions, it violates Article 14 and the mandate of Article 124.
3. Examine procedural compliance: Substantive and procedural requirements under the Constitution cannot be waived on mere grounds of administrative convenience.
4. Balance public interest vs constitutional discipline: Constitutional limitations always prevail over executive fiat.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Case Brief & Legal Assessment: Scope and Application of Article 124 (Establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court)
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE & CONSTITUTIONAL CONTEXT
Whether the State action, statutory enactment, or individual claim conforms to the constitutional mandate, procedural prerequisites, and substantive protections enshrined in Article 124 (Establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court) of the Constitution of India.

II. RULE & STATUTORY ANATOMY
Article 124 is situated in The Union (Articles 52–151), governing the “Union Judiciary” dimension of Indian constitutional law.
The essential constitutional ingredients are:
1. (1) There shall be a Supreme Court of India consisting of a Chief Justice of India and, until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number, of not more than [seven other Judges.
2. (2) Every Judge of the Supreme Court shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal on the recommendation of the National Judicial Appointments Commission referred to in article 124A and shall hold office until he attains the age of sixty-five years: [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted Provided that]—
3. (a) a Judge may, by writing under his hand addressed to the President, resign his office;
4. (b) a Judge may be removed from his office in the manner

III. PROCEDURAL ANCHOR & REMEDIAL FORUM
1. Competent Forum: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Standard of Review: Ultra vires doctrine, legislative competence (Lists I, II, III of Seventh Schedule), non-arbitrariness under Article 14, and procedural vires.
3. Standing: Aggrieved party whose legal, statutory, or constitutional rights are infringed, or public-spirited person in representative actions where public interest is directly affected.

IV. JUDICIAL INTERPRETATION & AUTHORITY
In Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) (2016) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court established that Struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act. Judicial primacy in appointments is part of the basic structure. The collegium system revived.
Furthermore, in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625, the Court reaffirmed that constitutional guarantees are justiciable and binding upon all state functionaries.

V. APPLICATION TO FACT PATTERNS
To apply Article 124:
1. Verify whether the impugned measure falls within the scope of the article's textual command.
2. Check whether any express exceptions, provisos, or constitutional limitations apply.
3. Subject the measure to tests of proportionality and non-arbitrariness under Article 14. If an ingredient is missing or breached, the measure is unconstitutional.

VI. CONCLUSION
Article 124 stands as a vital constitutional checkpoint. Any state action in breach thereof is void and amenable to writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226. Current through the 106th Amendment (2023).

questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. INTRODUCTION & CONSTITUTIONAL PHILOSOPHY
Article 124 of the Constitution of India, titled “Establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court”, represents a critical cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. Situated within The Union (Articles 52–151), the provision balances state power with individual liberties and institutional accountability. The Constituent Assembly intended this provision to be an active, living guarantee rather than an ornamental declaration.
II. STATUTORY & DOCTRINAL DECONSTRUCTION
A forensic analysis of Article 124 reveals the following distinct constitutional limbs:
(a) Limb 1: (1) There shall be a Supreme Court of India consisting of a Chief Justice of India and, until Parliament by law prescribes a larger number, of not more than [seven other Judges.
(a) Limb 2: (2) Every Judge of the Supreme Court shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal on the recommendation of the National Judicial Appointments Commission referred to in article 124A and shall hold office until he attains the age of sixty-five years: [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted [omitted Provided that]—
(a) Limb 3: (a) a Judge may, by writing under his hand addressed to the President, resign his office;
(a) Limb 4: (b) a Judge may be removed from his office in the manner
The Article must be read in conjunction with the foundational architecture of the Constitution:
1. Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances: No branch of government possesses untrammelled discretion.
2. Rule of Law & Non-Arbitrariness: Every exercise of authority under Article 124 must satisfy the basic standard of fairness and reasonableness.
3. Transformative Constitutionalism: The provision must be interpreted progressively to advance justice, liberty, and equality as pledged in the Preamble.
III. JURISPRUDENTIAL EVOLUTION & LEADING CASE LAW
The Supreme Court of India has deconstructed Article 124 across several seminal judgments:
1. Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) (2016) 5 SCC 1:
   Ratio Decidendi: Struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act. Judicial primacy in appointments is part of the basic structure. The collegium system revived.
2. Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) (1980) 3 SCC 625:
   Ratio Decidendi: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles form the bedrock of the Constitution; institutional boundaries and constitutional discipline cannot be breached.
IV. PROCEDURAL ROADMAP & LITIGATION CHECKLIST (SENIOR COUNSEL REFERENCE)
When approaching the Court under or in respect of Article 124:
1. Forum Selection: High Court under Article 226 (judicial review of legislative and executive action, challenge to vires) and Supreme Court under Article 136 (Special Leave Petition) / Article 32 (if fundamental rights are violated).
2. Pleading Essentials: The writ petition or plaint must specifically plead:
   (a) The exact constitutional authority or violation under Article 124;
   (b) The factual narrative establishing how each statutory ingredient is satisfied or infringed;
   (c) The absence of an effective alternative remedy, or justification under the Whirlpool Corporation exceptions (breach of fundamental rights, violation of natural justice, or complete lack of jurisdiction).
3. Evidentiary Standard: Discharge of burden under BSA ss. 104–106 and production of certified records.
V. IRAC PROBLEM ANALYSIS (PRACTICE HYPOTHETICAL)
Fact Matrix: The State issues a notification encroaching upon the domain of Article 124 without satisfying statutory preconditions.
Issue: Does the executive notification violate the constitutional guarantees and procedures of Article 124?
Rule: Under Article 124, state action is strictly conditioned by constitutional provisions and cannot be exercised arbitrarily.
Application: The impugned notification fails because it circumvents the procedural safeguards and lacks rational nexus to the constitutional objective. Applying the proportionality test, the State has failed to adopt the least intrusive means.
Conclusion: The notification is unconstitutional and void ab initio. The appropriate writ of certiorari or mandamus shall issue.
VI. CRITICAL APPRAISAL & CURRENT-LAW MILESTONE
Article 124 remains a vibrant instrument of governance, current through the 106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023. A robust democracy requires rigorous adherence to its letter and spirit to protect the citizen against executive overreach and legislative excesses.

enhancement.definition: Article 124 governs the establishment, composition, appointment, qualifications, tenure, oath, and removal of Judges of the Supreme Court of India. It establishes the Supreme Court as the apex judicial tribunal of the Republic and sets forth the constitutional procedure for judicial appointments, interpreted by Constitution Benches to vest primacy in the judicial collegium headed by the Chief Justice of India to safeguard judicial independence.

essentialIngredients: Composition (Clause 1): A Chief Justice of India and such number of other Judges as Parliament may by law prescribe (currently 34).

Appointment (Clause 2): Every Judge of the Supreme Court is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal after 'consultation' with such Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts as the President may deem necessary.

Mandatory Collegium Primacy: In appointing other Judges, the Chief Justice of India MUST always be consulted; 'consultation' means 'concurrence' of a Collegium comprising the CJI and the four senior-most puisne judges (Second and Third Judges Cases).

Qualifications (Clause 3): A citizen of India who has been: (a) A High Court Judge for at least 5 years; OR (b) An advocate of a High Court for at least 10 years; OR (c) In the opinion of the President, a distinguished jurist.
Tenure: Holds office until attaining the age of sixty-five (65) years.

Removal Procedure (Clause 4): Can only be removed by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a special majority (majority of total membership + 2/3rd present and voting) on grounds of proven misbehaviour or incapacity.
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Article 124 is the constitutional pillar safeguarding the independence of the Indian judiciary.

### 1. The Evolution of the Collegium System
The interpretation of the word **'consultation'** in Article 124(2) led to a historic constitutional struggle:
- **First Judges Case (S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, 1981):** A 7-judge bench held that 'consultation' does NOT mean 'concurrence'. The executive had ultimate primacy in appointments, provided consultation was meaningful.
- **Second Judges Case (Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Assn., 1993):** A 9-judge bench overruled S.P. Gupta, holding that 'consultation' means **concurrence**. To protect judicial independence (a basic feature), primacy in judicial appointments was vested in the Chief Justice of India, acting in consultation with his two senior-most colleagues.
- **Third Judges Case (Special Reference No. 1 of 1998):** On a presidential reference under Article 143, the Supreme Court clarified the collegium structure: for Supreme Court appointments, the CJI must consult a collegium of the **four senior-most puisne judges** of the Supreme Court. An appointment recommended without following the collegium process is not binding on the Government.

### 2. The NJAC Case (Fourth Judges Case, 2016)
Parliament enacted the **Constitution (Ninety-ninth Amendment) Act, 2014** and the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) Act, 2014, replacing the Collegium with a 6-member commission comprising the CJI, two senior SC judges, the Union Law Minister, and two eminent persons.
In *Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Assn. v. Union of India (2016)*, a 5-judge Constitution Bench by a 4:1 majority struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act as unconstitutional and void, holding that:
1. The Independence of the Judiciary is an essential part of the **Basic Structure**;
2. Primacy of the judiciary in appointments is an indispensable component of judicial independence;
3. The inclusion of the Law Minister and civil society vetoes damaged judicial independence.
The Collegium system was consequently revived and restored.

### 3. Removal of Judges (Article 124(4) & (5))
A Supreme Court judge enjoys security of tenure and cannot be removed at the pleasure of the executive. Removal requires a rigorous constitutional procedure: an investigation by a committee of three jurists under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, followed by an address passed by both Houses of Parliament with a double special majority in the same session, on grounds strictly limited to **proven misbehaviour or incapacity** (*Sub-Committee on Judicial Accountability v. Union of India*).
examples: Executive Attempt to Bypass Collegium Recommendation: The Collegium unanimously recommends a senior High Court Chief Justice for elevation to the Supreme Court. The Union Government returns the recommendation for reconsideration. The Collegium unanimously reiterates the name. Under the Second and Third Judges Cases, the reiterated recommendation is binding on the executive, which must process the appointment.

Removal Motion for Proven Misbehavior: An impeachment motion is admitted against a sitting judge for financial misappropriation. A three-member inquiry committee under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 records a finding of proven misbehavior. The motion is debated in Parliament. It must secure a majority of the total membership of each House AND a 2/3rd majority of members present and voting for the President to issue an order of removal under Article 124(4).
distinctions: Supreme Court Appointment (Art. 124) vs High Court Appointment (Art. 217): Supreme Court judges are appointed on the advice of a 5-member collegium (CJI + 4 senior SC judges); High Court judges are appointed on the advice of a 3-member collegium (CJI + 2 senior SC judges), in consultation with the State Governor and the Chief Justice of that High Court.

Impeachment of President (Art. 61) vs Removal of Judge (Art. 124(4)): Presidential impeachment requires a 2/3rd majority of the *total membership* of each House; removal of a Supreme Court judge requires a majority of the total membership AND a 2/3rd majority of *members present and voting*.
problemApplication: Issue: Parliament passes a statute authorizing the Prime Minister to directly appoint any distinguished jurist as Chief Justice of India without consulting the Collegium or the outgoing Chief Justice. Is the statute constitutionally valid?

Rule: Under Article 124(2) as interpreted in the Second Judges Case, Third Judges Case, and the NJAC ruling, judicial primacy in appointment and consultation with the CJI is an integral part of the Basic Structure.
Application: Bypassing the Chief Justice and Collegium to confer unilateral appointment power on the Executive directly destroys the Independence of the Judiciary, violating the basic structure.
Counterargument: The Government argues that Article 124(1) empowers Parliament to regulate the Supreme Court by law and that popular mandate justifies executive selection.
Conclusion: The statute is ultra vires Article 124 and void ab initio for violating the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
